prize_parts.citation: for the development of optical lattice clocks, from the magic-wavelength concept to fractional uncertainties at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Four of eight colleagues placed B022 first and six ranked it in their top three, which I do not treat as merit by itself; the merit is that the lattice clock is a single clean idea (magic-wavelength trapping, which removes Doppler and recoil shifts while keeping thousands of atoms interrogated) followed by exhaustive control of every systematic. It has been reproduced and exceeded at JILA, Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE and NIST, with clock-to-clock agreement at the 10^-18 level, and it has already delivered new physics: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, limits on varying constants and ultralight dark matter, and a many-body (Fermi-degenerate) regime of metrology. Katori carries the concept and the first demonstrations, Ye the decisive path to the record regime, so two names is a clean and defensible allocation. It also differs from 2005 (frequency comb) and 2012 (single ion control), since those prizes enabled the clock rather than recognising the lattice architecture.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that precision metrology can be read as an engineering refinement of laser cooling, combs and ion clocks that were already honoured, and that the societal endorsement (redefinition of the SI second) is still pending. Credit also spreads beyond two names: Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom and the ion-clock groups all shaped the field, and I cannot resolve the finer priority questions from the packet alone. If the committee judges the contribution as a tool rather than a discovery, B020 is the more conceptually rich alternative.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B022 first because the discovery is unambiguous, with tests of relativity at the millimetre scale, searches for varying constants and dark matter, and a path to redefining the second, and he sees it as distinct from the earlier comb and ion-clock prizes.
responses.response: I agree on the science and on the separation from 2005 and 2012, but I would argue it more specifically: the new element is the combination of many-atom interrogation with magic-wavelength trapping, which changes the statistical limit, whereas the earlier prizes covered the comb and single-ion control. I am more cautious than Ulf on the dark-matter and constants searches, which so far give limits and not detections, so the citation should rest on the demonstrated precision and the redshift measurements and not on prospective discoveries.

responses.point: Olsson places B038 (tunnel magnetoresistance) first as an original experimental discovery with large technological consequences, and ranks B022 third as an enabling tool whose redefinition of the second is still pending.
responses.response: I take the point on B038 seriously: room-temperature TMR is a clear effect that was reproduced everywhere and is well understood through symmetry-filtered tunnelling. My reservations are the overlap with the 2007 GMR prize and, more concretely, that the MgO giant-TMR credit sits partly with Yuasa and Djayaprawira outside the credited names, so a fair three-person configuration is hard. On her worry that B022 is a tool awaiting the redefinition, I disagree that we must wait: the 10^-18 agreement between independent labs is already the scientific result, and the SI decision follows from it rather than validating it.

responses.point: Pearce ranks B002 (IceCube) first because opening a new observational window with a purpose-built instrument is the achievement he respects most, and he finds a one-person prize for Halzen defensible.
responses.response: I share the value on opening a new window, and the diffuse flux is well established. But I am less comfortable than Mark about a single-name prize for a large collaboration whose source identifications (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068) are still at the 3 to 4 sigma level and where AMANDA-era and collaboration leaders such as Botner, Karle and Spiering would be left out. Astroparticle physics is outside my expertise, so I defer on the strength of the evidence, but on attribution maturity B022 seems the safer and fairer configuration to me.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B022 first and B004 (atom interferometry) second, arguing that progress is limited by measurement precision and that real instruments are in use, but notes that three of the four credited names for B004 forces a hard allocation.
responses.response: I agree with the first-place logic, and I think his own attribution caveat for B004 is exactly why I rank B022 above it: Pritchard, Bordé, Kasevich and Schmiedmayer all have strong claims, and Chu's absence from the credited list leaves an awkward gap, whereas B022 resolves cleanly to two. The fundamental-physics reach of long-baseline atom interferometry is also still largely prospective.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B018 (dynamical mean-field theory) first and B028 second, and places B014 (circuit QED) seventh partly because of its proximity to the 2025 prize and because it may be infrastructure.
responses.response: On B014 we are in broad agreement about the 2025 overlap, and I would add that I rank it with my proximity to the field in mind, so I would prefer the committee to weigh it without leaning on my view. On B018 I side with Mehlig that DMFT is a method rather than a phenomenon, and the missing Metzner credit is a real problem; I am therefore not persuaded it should outrank a measured, reproduced result like B022.

uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers to wait for the SI second redefinition as an external endorsement of the lattice clock.

Whether two names fully capture the credit for the lattice clock, given Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom and others, and whether the citation should centre on the architecture or on the 10^-18 performance.
If B022 does not carry, whether B020 can be resolved among five credited names (Bloch, Cirac, Greiner, Zoller, Esslinger) without arbitrary exclusions.
statement.conflict_note: My preferred configuration (B022) involves no specific connection from my profile. I do declare a conflict regarding B014 (circuit QED), as a theorist in superconducting circuits, director of WACQT and a colleague of Chalmers groups (Delsing, Wilson), and I would recuse myself from deliberation and voting on that entry. WACQT's ties to Lund and KTH and Chalmers hosting the 2025 laureates are not connected to B022, B020 or B043.
